title: Thermal Cycling, Extreme PCR, Fold-Change Math and the eSensor Readout
summary: Follow one PCR cycle to the Ct, calculate fold change from efficiency and the Ct difference, see how rapid-cycle and extreme PCR cut run time, and read the GenMark eSensor electrochemical cutoff.

locations.section: Calculation Check: Ct and Fold Change

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 69 Hits 14 and 15, the Calculation Check (Ct and fold change) and the Figure (thermal cycling to amplified product; Ct anchor). Checked against Kralik 2017, Bustin 2020, Svec 2015, Millington 2019, Farrar 2015 (abstract only), Ruijter 2009 (full text), Pfaffl 2001 (abstract only), Muller 2026, Bustin 2026, Parker 2015 (full text) and Pierce 2012 (abstract only; its methods were seen only as a page-fetch summary and not relied on). Hit 14 calls extreme PCR “rapid-cycle” PCR; the sources treat rapid cycle (1991, 10–30 min for 30 cycles) and extreme PCR (2015, 15–60 s) as separate speed classes, and the reviewer’s “40 cycles in ≤30 minutes in thin-walled capillaries” was not found in the sources read, so it is not taught. Hit 15’s 3 nA cutoff is taught as the respiratory viral panel rule on the XT-8 from Parker 2015; Hit 15’s word “voltammetric” is not taught because the source read describes a measured current. The worked fold-change numbers are arithmetic applying the source formula. Not taught: the Number Vault table, Taq processivity, other eSensor panels.

objectives: Describe the steps of a PCR cycle and why more starting template gives a lower Ct.
Calculate fold change from the amplification efficiency and the Ct difference.
Distinguish rapid-cycle PCR from extreme PCR and state what makes extreme PCR fast.
State how the GenMark eSensor respiratory viral panel detects targets and its positivity cutoff.

scenes.title: Three numbers on one bench
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a molecular bench shows three readouts. Card 1: a real-time PCR sample crosses threshold at Ct 22 while the calibrator crosses at Ct 25, efficiency (E) 1.96. Card 2: a research protocol claims 35 PCR cycles in under a minute. Card 3: an electrochemical respiratory panel reports 4.5 nA for one target and 1.2 nA for another. Question token: “How much more template? How so fast? Which target is positive?”

cues.text: Invented scenario. A real-time PCR sample crosses the threshold at cycle twenty-two; the calibrator crosses at cycle twenty-five.
A research protocol claims thirty-five PCR cycles in under a minute. And an electrochemical respiratory panel reports one target at four point five nanoamps and another at one point two.
How much more template is in the sample? How can PCR run that fast? And which target is positive?

props.label: How much more? How so fast? Which is positive?

scenes.title: One cycle, then forty
scenes.altText: Schematic of a thermal cycler run. Three step cards in a row: Denature (heat; the two DNA strands separate), Anneal (cool; primers and probe bind the single strands), Extend (the polymerase copies each strand). A counter card: at 100% efficiency the copies double every cycle, Nn = N0 × (1 + E)^n; a typical real-time run repeats the cycle about 40 times. A Ct card: the more template at the start, the fewer cycles to reach the threshold; Ct plotted against log starting amount is a straight line with a negative slope, about −3.33 per 10-fold at 100% efficiency.

cues.text: Each PCR cycle has the same steps. Heat denatures the template, separating the two strands. Cooling lets the primers, and any probe, anneal to the single strands.
Then the polymerase extends the primers, copying each strand. Many protocols combine annealing and extension into one step.
At one hundred percent efficiency the number of copies doubles every cycle, and a typical real-time run repeats the cycle about forty times.
The more template at the start, the fewer cycles it takes to cross the threshold. Plot Ct against the log of the starting amount and you get a straight line with a negative slope.

props.title: Ct and starting amount
lines: Ct vs log amount: negative slope

scenes.title: From hours to seconds
scenes.altText: Speed ladder of PCR classes (Millington 2019, Table 1), time for 30 cycles: Legacy (1988) about 2.25 hours, with about 90% of the time spent ramping between temperatures; Rapid cycle (1991), in capillaries, 10–30 minutes; Fast (2000s) 30–60 minutes; Ultra-fast (2010s) 2–10 minutes; Extreme (2015) 15–60 seconds with 0.5–2-second cycles. A second card: how extreme PCR gets there (Farrar 2015 abstract): primer and polymerase concentrations raised 10- to 20-fold, 0.4–2.0-second cycles, efficiency above 90%, specific single products; PCR time is inversely related to the concentration of critical reactants.

cues.text: Speed is measured as the time for thirty cycles. Legacy PCR in 1988 took about two and a quarter hours, and about ninety percent of that time was spent ramping between temperatures.

Rapid cycle PCR, introduced in 1991 and run in capillaries, cut thirty cycles to ten to thirty minutes. Extreme PCR, reported in 2015, runs thirty cycles in fifteen to sixty seconds, with cycles of half a second to two seconds.
Faster heating alone is not enough. Extreme PCR raised primer and polymerase concentrations ten- to twenty-fold, so annealing and extension keep pace with the faster cycles.
The result was efficient, specific amplification of short targets: efficiencies above ninety percent and single products. PCR time is inversely related to the concentration of the critical reactants.

scenes.title: Fold change and the eSensor readout
scenes.altText: Left card, efficiency scale: E runs from 1 to 2, where 2 means 100% (doubling); efficiency is derived from the standard-curve slope; relative quantity = E^−Cq, so a sample that crosses ΔCt cycles earlier holds E^ΔCt times more template. Worked: Ct 22 vs 25 at E 1.96 → 1.96³ ≈ 7.5× more; 4 cycles earlier at E 2.0 → 2⁴ = 16× more; 2 cycles later at E 1.9 → 1.9² ≈ 3.6× less. Right card, GenMark eSensor respiratory viral panel (Parker 2015): multiplex PCR, exonuclease digestion to single-stranded DNA, ferrocene-labelled signal probe, capture probe on a gold electrode, current measured; on the XT-8 instrument a target is detected with confidence at 3 nA or more. Hook answers: about 7.5× more; extreme PCR with high primer and polymerase; target A positive (4.5 nA), target B not (1.2 nA).

cues.text: Now the math. On this scale efficiency runs from one to two, where two means perfect doubling. It comes from the standard-curve slope, and each sample’s relative quantity is the efficiency raised to minus its Ct.

So a sample that crosses three cycles earlier at an efficiency of one point nine six has one point nine six cubed, about seven and a half times more template. At perfect efficiency, four cycles earlier is sixteen-fold; two cycles later at one point nine is about three point six times less.

The GenMark eSensor respiratory panel reads amplified DNA electrically. After PCR, an exonuclease makes the product single-stranded; it binds a ferrocene-labelled signal probe and is captured on a gold electrode, where the resulting current is measured.
In that panel, a target is detected with confidence when its signal is three nanoamps or more. So target A at four point five nanoamps is positive, and target B at one point two is not.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Rapid-cycle PCR and extreme PCR are the same thing” (✓ rapid cycle: 10–30 min for 30 cycles in capillaries; extreme: 15–60 s with 10–20× primer and polymerase); “Fold change is always 2^ΔCt” (✓ use the measured efficiency: 1.96³ ≈ 7.5, not 8; efficiency errors distort fold change); “The eSensor reads fluorescence” (✓ it measures an electrochemical current at a gold electrode; ≥3 nA is positive in the respiratory viral panel).

cues.text: Trap one: rapid-cycle PCR and extreme PCR are the same thing. No: rapid cycle takes ten to thirty minutes for thirty cycles; extreme PCR takes fifteen to sixty seconds and needs much higher primer and polymerase concentrations.

Trap two: fold change is always two to the power of the Ct difference. No: use the measured efficiency. Three cycles at one point nine six is about seven and a half, not eight, and a wrong efficiency distorts the result.
Trap three: the eSensor reads fluorescence. No: it measures an electrical current at a gold electrode, and three nanoamps or more is positive in its respiratory panel.

scenes.title: The copier race
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “PCR is a copier race. Every lap through the copier doubles the pile, so the bigger the starting pile, the sooner it hits the ceiling (low Ct). To run laps in seconds you must stack far more paper and toner (primers and polymerase). The eSensor weighs the finished pile by electric current: 3 nA tips the scale.” Tokens: lap = cycle · ceiling = threshold · paper and toner = primers and polymerase · scale = current. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: PCR is a copier race. Every lap doubles the pile, so a bigger starting pile hits the ceiling sooner, which is a low Ct. To run laps in seconds you must stack far more paper and toner, the primers and polymerase. The eSensor weighs the pile by current, and three nanoamps tips the scale.

Where it breaks: real efficiency is usually a little below perfect doubling; extreme speed also needs accurate temperature control and short products; and the three-nanoamp cutoff comes from one panel’s rule, so check the assay’s own instructions.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Lower Ct = more template · fold change = E^ΔCt (E 2 = 100%)”, “Rapid cycle 10–30 min · extreme 15–60 s with 10–20× primer and polymerase · eSensor RVP ≥3 nA = positive”.

cues.text: A lower Ct means more starting template and the fold difference is the efficiency raised to the Ct difference, extreme PCR reaches fifteen to sixty seconds only by raising primer and polymerase concentrations, and the eSensor respiratory panel calls a target positive at three nanoamps or more.

props.label: Lower Ct = more template · fold change = E^ΔCt (E 2 = 100%)
Extreme PCR 15–60 s needs 10–20× reactants · eSensor ≥ 3 nA

explanation.what: Plain language: PCR copies DNA by heating and cooling it over and over; each round roughly doubles the copies, so a sample with more DNA reaches a visible signal in fewer rounds. Faster machines and richer reaction mixes shrink the run from hours to seconds, and one panel reads its result as an electric current instead of light. Scientific terms: denaturation, annealing, extension, amplification efficiency (E), quantification cycle (Ct or Cq), standard curve slope, relative quantity, fold change, rapid cycle PCR, extreme PCR, exonuclease, ferrocene label, gold electrode, electrochemical current, nanoampere (nA).
explanation.why: PCR is exponential, so the starting amount sets how many cycles are needed to cross a threshold, and the efficiency sets how much each cycle multiplies the product. Cycle speed is limited by temperature changes and by how fast primers anneal and polymerase extends; raising primer and polymerase concentrations speeds those reactions.
explanation.measure: Nn = N0 × (1 + E)^n with E as a fraction (100% = doubling); as a fraction, E = 10^(−1/slope) − 1. On the 1–2 scale (2 = 100%), relative quantity = E^−Ct, so fold change = E^ΔCt. Slope about −3.33 per 10-fold dilution at 100%. Time for 30 cycles: legacy about 2.25 h; rapid cycle 10–30 min; extreme 15–60 s (primers and polymerase 10–20× higher, cycles 0.4–2.0 s). eSensor respiratory viral panel on the XT-8 instrument: signal ≥3 nA for a target = confident detection (positive).
explanation.differs: Rapid cycle PCR (1991, capillaries, minutes) vs extreme PCR (2015, seconds, high reactant concentrations); 2^ΔCt (assumes perfect doubling) vs efficiency-corrected E^ΔCt; fluorescence real-time detection vs eSensor electrochemical detection after PCR.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: compute fold change from a Ct difference and efficiency, recognise that a lower Ct means more template, identify what makes extreme PCR fast, or recognise the eSensor’s electrochemical readout and 3 nA cutoff.

questions.stem: A sample crosses the threshold at Ct 22 and the calibrator at Ct 25. Amplification efficiency is 1.96 (on a scale where 2 means perfect doubling). How much template does the sample have relative to the calibrator?

options.rationale: Correct. Fold change = E^ΔCt = 1.96³ ≈ 7.5, and the lower Ct means more template.
Incorrect. A lower Ct means the threshold was reached sooner because there was more starting template.
Incorrect. That multiplies efficiency by the Ct difference; PCR is exponential, so the efficiency is raised to the power of the difference.
Incorrect. Eight-fold assumes perfect doubling (E = 2); with the measured E of 1.96 the answer is about 7.5.

questions.stem: Extreme PCR amplifies short targets in 15–60 seconds. Besides very short temperature cycles, what change made this possible?

options.text: Primer and polymerase concentrations raised 10- to 20-fold
options.rationale: Correct. Higher primer and polymerase concentrations let annealing and extension keep pace with 0.4–2.0-second cycles.

options.text: Running the reaction at a single constant temperature
options.rationale: Incorrect. Extreme PCR still cycles between denaturation and annealing/extension temperatures.
Incorrect. Extreme PCR still uses denaturation temperatures in every cycle.
Incorrect. A 60-bp target was amplified in 14.7 s using 35 cycles; speed came from short cycles, not few cycles.

questions.stem: On the GenMark eSensor respiratory viral panel, which result is interpreted as positive for a target?

options.text: An electrochemical current of 3 nA or greater for that target
options.rationale: Correct. On the XT-8 instrument, a target is detected with confidence when its signal is 3 nA or more.

options.text: A fluorescence curve crossing the threshold during cycling
options.rationale: Incorrect. That describes real-time fluorescence PCR; the eSensor measures current at gold electrodes.

options.text: A signal of 0.3 nA or greater
options.rationale: Incorrect. The cutoff in the panel is 3 nA, ten times higher.
Incorrect. A defined cutoff (3 nA) separates positive from negative signals.

claims.text: Speed classes: legacy about 2.25 h, rapid cycle 10–30 min in capillaries, ultra-fast 2–10 min, extreme 15–60 s per 30 cycles; legacy time mostly ramping.
Extreme PCR: primer and polymerase 10–20× higher, 0.4–2.0 s cycles, efficiency above 90%, single products, 35 cycles in 14.7 s; time inversely related to reactant concentration.
eSensor respiratory viral panel: PCR, exonuclease to single strand, ferrocene signal probe, gold-electrode capture, current measured; ≥3 nA = confident detection on the XT-8.

accuracyFlags.issue: Hit 14 labels extreme PCR as “rapid-cycle” PCR and gives “40 cycles in ≤30 minutes in thin-walled capillaries”. Millington 2019 lists rapid cycle PCR (1991, capillaries, 10–30 min for 30 cycles) and extreme PCR (2015, 15–60 s) as separate speed classes; the 40-cycle figure and “thin-walled” were not found in the sources read. The lesson teaches the two classes separately.

Hit 15 states the 3 nA cutoff for “GenMark eSensor” generally. Parker 2015 gives it for the GenMark respiratory viral panel on the XT-8 instrument (detected with confidence at or above 3 nA) and describes the readout as a measured current, not specifically voltammetry; whether other eSensor panels use the same cutoff was not verified, so the lesson ties the cutoff to that panel.
